item.title: Free e-government platform that serves two billion people in ten countries has critical SQL injection bug
item.description: India’s Digital Infrastructure for Governance Impact and Transformation tool can leak data
item.content:encoded: India’s free e-government platform has a critical SQL injection flaw that thousands of organizations must patch to protect up to two billion citizens. The platform is called the Digital Infrastructure for Governance (Impact and Transformation) – aka DIGIT – and is a modular suite that offers common services such as authentication and payment collection. Third party developers can also create DIGIT modules, and plenty have done so and now offer add-ons that handle tasks as diverse as managing birth and death certificates, revenue collection, and running water treatment plants. DIGIT is ubiquitous in India, where all state and union territory governments use the platform, as do over 20,000 local government entities. India also exports DIGIT under its policy of turning software created for its own needs into “digital public goods” (DPI) that it happily gives away to other nations. Nine nations have implemented DIGIT to some degree, among them Mozambique, Liberia, Senegal, Nigeria, Burundi, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Jamaica, and Sri Lanka India’s population is 1.4 billion. Indonesia’s is 280 million and Nigeria is home to 240 million. DIGIT is therefore used by governments that serve over two billion people, some of whom are now at risk thanks to CVE-2026-136706, a 9.3-rated SQL injection flaw present in DIGIT which allows “improper neutralization of user supplied input while constructing SQL queries and execution in the affected User and Access Control Service components.” “An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending specially crafted input through the affected API endpoint to the targeted system,” according to CERT-IN. “Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary SQL queries, potentially resulting in unauthorized disclosure, modification or deletion of database information on the targeted system.” eGov India, which oversees work on DIGIT, has released source code for an update that fixes the problem. While local government users of DIGIT typically access it as SaaS, through large implementations run by national or state governments, over 1,000 deployments are live across various cities and other entities. Those orgs can therefore add patching DIGIT to their urgent to-do lists, along with fixing Java, PHP, vCenter and any other widely used technologies that suddenly need an urgent security update. ®

item.title: Microsoft: Hackers in China, N Korea using ARTEX AI tool to break into global tech systems
item.description: Agentic offensive framework automates familiar attack techniques, with weak defenses potentially breached in minutes
item.content:encoded: Chinese and North Korean state-sponsored hacking crews are among the growing number of groups known for using the ARTEX pentesting tool in attacks, Microsoft said this week. ARTEX is an open source, AI-powered penetration testing framework that attackers have adopted to automate reconnaissance, credential attacks, and exploitation since its public release in July. Campaigns that have been linked to ARTEX have targeted cloud environments, IT software like ConnectWise, and financial institutions globally, sometimes reaching privileged access in under three hours. Salt Typhoon is arguably the most recognizable name on the list of ARTEX beneficiaries – the group responsible for attacks on telcos AT&T and Verizon, US government systems, UK prime minister's aides, and more. The lesser-known Crystal Typhoon – the group behind the ArcaneDoor attacks back when Microsoft called it Storm-1849 – was also named alongside it, as were North Korea's Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet. Microsoft also named China-state-aligned Storm-0940, linked to the ConnectWise compromise, and financially motivated, Cambodia-based Storm-3358. It had previously reported both groups' use of ARTEX. Chinese cybersecurity company ThreatBook claimed ownership of ARTEX in November. GitHub user "Autumn-27" originally published its source code with a Chinese-language interface in July. Various forks of the repo, which was taken down in October, have meant that the same framework is available in multiple languages. According to Infrawatch, there are more than 130 variants of ARTEX in circulation, and it is the most widely used agentic offensive framework (AOF) at present. Like other offensive security tools adopted by criminals, ARTEX can lower the effort required to mount attacks. Experienced groups can also use it to automate repetitive work and pursue multiple avenues at once. As Microsoft echoed this week, after the FBI and AWS issued their warnings earlier this month, ARTEX is proving to be a useful tool for the more sophisticated groups to streamline and hasten their attacks too. It's being used to help attackers steal AI and cloud credentials at "industrial scale," as AWS put it, which provide attackers access to advanced models for free. Microsoft says ARTEX can progress from reconnaissance to persistent, privileged access within minutes, depending on its configuration and the target's defenses. "In the past few weeks, we've reported several distinct campaigns that abused ARTEX to search public repositories for exposed secrets, enable supply chain compromise, and scan internet-facing systems for exploitation," its threat intelligence team blogged. "These campaigns illustrate how threat actors use ARTEX to automate various stages of the attack chain. "Threat actors define scope and targets for ARTEX, which then uses AI agents to set verifiable goals, define tactical steps for each stage of the operation, use tools to attack targets, create graphs to track discovered systems and results of actions, and report back to the threat actor." Notably, ARTEX does not offer any new attack techniques. All of the tool's capabilities were previously known to the cybersecurity world, but its value lies in the automation capabilities it offers users, chaining attacks at machine speed. In the UK NCSC's warning about AOFs this week, it said the key strengths of this technology are its speed, its thoroughness in probing target systems for weaknesses, how it learns from failures instantly, and that it is inexpensive to run at scale. AOFs' speed comes at a cost, however. These tools are noisy, the NCSC said, making them easier to detect in network logs and by defensive solutions. Some examples of the attacks in which the tool has been implicated include Storm-0940's hit on ConnectWise, which enabled attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, various financial institutions in South Korea and India, UK registrar 123 Reg, and the European Commission. ®

item.title: UK privacy watchdog faces probe into its workplace culture
item.description: Independent review will examine leadership, accountability, and how staff concerns were handled before former commissioner John Edwards resigned
item.content:encoded: Britain's privacy watchdog is getting a taste of its own medicine, with an independent review set to examine the culture, governance, and accountability surrounding the events that led to former Information Commissioner John Edwards' resignation. Karon Monaghan KC will examine whether the regulator's culture and governance allowed problems to develop or made concerns harder to raise. Edwards quit in June after an independent workplace investigation found there was a "case to answer" over his behavior and that his conduct fell short of what was expected of a public official. He disagreed with some of its findings, but ultimately conceded that he had shown "poor judgment." That investigation, however, focused on Edwards alone. According to the terms of reference published on Thursday, it "did not consider the wider conditions in which that conduct occurred, and it was not designed to." The new review will cast a wider net. Monaghan wants to know whether staff could call out bad behavior further up the food chain, and what awaited those who tried. It will also poke around the regulator's leadership and governance arrangements and its relationship with its sponsoring government department, including whether there were adequate ways for concerns to be escalated and those at the top to be challenged. Current and former staff can give evidence confidentially and voluntarily, while Monaghan will be given access to relevant documents and existing material, including staff surveys and data on bullying, harassment and discrimination. The ICO has confirmed it won't use confidentiality clauses in settlement agreements to prevent people from contributing to the review. Monaghan decides which witnesses and documents are relevant, rather than the ICO or DCMS. Access remains subject to legal restrictions, and she must be told when material is withheld and why. She can speak to whoever she thinks is relevant and ask for the complaints, correspondence, and other paperwork she needs. And if that leads her somewhere unexpected, she can ask to widen the investigation. DCMS can refuse, but it won't be able to quietly brush the request aside, and any decision not to expand the scope has to make it into the final report. The review won't reopen the investigation into Edwards, make findings about the conduct of named individuals, or delve into the merits of the regulator's enforcement decisions. Its arrival comes amid a broader shake-up at Britain's data watchdog. The old Information Commissioner's Office was formally replaced by the Information Commission on September 30, bringing with it a new board-led governance model. The government first promised the wider review in July, shortly after Edwards' departure, but it didn't appoint its reviewer or nail down the terms until late November. "We need to understand what is working, where things are falling short and, crucially, what needs to change," said DCMS Secretary Lisa Nandy. The watchdog won't have to wait long for its report card. Monaghan is expected to deliver her findings in the first quarter of 2027, after which they will be published and handed to Parliament. ®

item.title: 'Significant number of customer records' pwned in Flight Centre Travel Group breach
item.description: The latest attack in spate of similar incidents targeting booking systems globally
item.content:encoded: Travel giant Flight Centre Travel Group (FLT) says "a significant number of customer records" may have been accessed by "unknown persons" following a cyberattack. The Brisbane-headquartered company said the incident affected a third-party accommodation booking system used by Flight Centre, Travel Associates, Cruiseabout, and some independent travel agents. Its disclosure [PDF], filed with the Australian Securities Exchange today, added that it was aware that records were accessed, but cannot definitively say how many were exfiltrated. Flight Centre is working with the supplier and incident response specialist Mandiant to establish the scope of the incident. An initial review suggests most accessed records contained only customer names, some with basic travel information. A "very small percentage" may also include birth dates, email addresses, limited passport details, phone numbers, or, in rare cases, health or mobility information. Flight bookings and corporate travel use separate systems and are unaffected, the company said. "FLT values customer privacy and data security," the company said in its disclosure. "The company understands that an incident like this can be unsettling for customers who may be affected, and we apologize for any concern this causes." Investigations remain ongoing, but FLT has already contained the attack, rotated keys and credentials, and increased system monitoring, it said. The company said it would contact affected customers directly. Its brands continue to operate normally, and travelers should proceed with their plans. Customers should independently verify unexpected messages about their bookings before clicking links, opening attachments, or sharing personal information. The attack on FLT follows others that have hit booking systems in the past year, including those on Booking.com and BWH Hotels. More recently, another Australian business, RMS Cloud, which provides booking software to travel and leisure companies, also acknowledged a breach that led to WhatsApp scams in late October. Numerous reports of travelers being targeted with messages that contained their names and booking details hit local news outlets at the time. Customers were sent convincing messages seemingly from the hotels they had booked, and according to Australia's National Anti-Scam Centre, the scams appeared to be financially motivated. Muhammad Yahya Patel, vCISO and cybersecurity advisor for EMEA at Huntress, said attackers targeting booking systems is a "familiar supply chain story" that has a greater impact than simple data theft. Speaking generally about the risks of exposed travel records, Patel said: "Unlike a compromised email address or phone number, a passport can't be changed easily or quickly. For affected customers, the practical risk extends well beyond the immediate breach. "Passport details combined with names, addresses, and travel history create a comprehensive identity profile that enables document fraud, identity theft, and targeted social engineering that could persist for years." ®

item.title: Wyoming uranium operation shuts down after cyberattack
item.description: Peninsula Energy says plant and wellfield control systems were affected, with no restart date yet
item.content:encoded: Peninsula Energy has temporarily shut down its Wyoming uranium operation after a "cybersecurity incident" affected plant and wellfield control systems. The Australian uranium producer said on Wednesday that it had activated its response procedures and brought in outside specialists following the attack on its US subsidiary, Strata Energy, which operates the Lance uranium project. Peninsula Energy said it believes the attack is "confined to the plant and wellfield operating and control systems," and that back-office functions, such as payroll and other corporate systems, in both the US and Australia, remain unaffected. "The company's immediate priorities have been to protect the safety of its employees, secure its operating systems, and work towards the restoration of operations in a safe and controlled manner," it said in an update to the Australian Securities Exchange. The notification [PDF] went on to say that Peninsula Energy's investigations into the attack, including whether any data was compromised, remain ongoing. Peninsula has not given a restart date and says it cannot yet assess the impact on its 2027 production guidance. Operations will remain suspended until recovery and safety checks are complete. "Peninsula will provide further updates to the market as material information becomes available," it said. The disclosure of additional information came two days after Peninsula secured a short trading halt, which referenced a cybersecurity incident at its Wyoming site. The November 23 filing [PDF] dated the incident to Friday evening in Western Australia. Wednesday's update clarified that Strata detected it on the morning of November 20, local US time. Peninsula subsequently requested a voluntary suspension of trading until the earlier of November 30 or an announcement on restarting operations and any resulting change to production guidance. Peninsula's Lance project is a uranium mining operation, extracting the element from underground deposits and turning it into uranium concentrate, aka yellowcake or U₃O₈. Uranium concentrate is feedstock for nuclear fuel production, typically undergoing conversion, enrichment, and fabrication into uranium dioxide pellets before use in reactors. The Lance central processing plant was constructed to produce a maximum of 2.0 million pounds (Mlb) of U₃O₈ annually, and is licensed for 3.0 Mlb. Peninsula previously forecast production of 500,000 to 600,000 pounds in 2027, having withdrawn its 2026 guidance earlier this year following operational problems at Lance. It now says it will reassess the 2027 outlook once operations resume. ®

item.title: Company was religious about backups but sinned by leaving them exposed
item.description: Never put the backup server in the same Windows domain as production
item.content:encoded: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we’re thankful every time someone leaves a password sticky note on a monitor or fails to delete a terminated employee’s admin account. But neither of those common occurrences is what we’ll be talking about today. Instead, our subject broke the number-one rule of backups: you gotta keep ’em separated. Our story comes courtesy of Da Li, who serves as global alliance manager at Info2Soft, a company that provides data protection and recovery software. At one point, a partner called him into a case where a Chinese vehicle parts manufacturer fell victim to a ransomware gang. Unfortunately, its backup was compromised too. The manufacturer had religiously backed up its manufacturing execution system (MES) and SAP orders, inventory, and finance systems every night. There was even a green dashboard that showed the backup process had succeeded, and someone checked that every morning. However, one Friday evening, crims broke into the network and found out that the backup server was joined to the same Windows domain as the rest of the network. The hackers found a plaintext password for the backup service account in a maintenance script on a file share and discovered that someone had used the very same password for a domain admin account. So the first thing the crooks did was delete every restore point on that backup server. Then they started encrypting the production servers to ransom them. “Every backup job had succeeded for three years,” Li said. “The failure was that the thing meant to save them could be reached with the same keys as the thing being attacked.” The results were devastating. With the MES and SAP data both gone, the plant couldn't schedule production, ship parts, or track them. By the time Li was called in, the plant had already resolved its ransomware situation. We don’t know whether it paid or not. The manufacturer did ask Li and his company to make sure that this couldn’t happen again. Li’s fix was not radical, but it was instructive. He made sure that the company now keeps its backup system outside the production domain, uses unique credentials, and requires MFA to reduce the risk of unauthorized access even if a password is compromised. He also made sure that the company keeps at least one offline backup and runs a test restore quarterly to ensure it’s prepared for emergencies.®

item.title: Hackers help themselves to 1Password's source code and customer data
item.description: An intruder planted malicious code in backend services, but the biz insists passwords are safe
item.content:encoded: 1Password is reassuring customers that their vaults remain secure after an attacker breached its systems and stole account information and private source code. The Canadian security biz disclosed this week that an attacker had compromised an employee's corporate GitHub account, made off with private source code, and deployed malicious code to its backend services to siphon off customer information. 1Password, which began investigating the intrusion on November 19, hasn't said how many customers were affected, but confirmed that the stolen data includes names and email addresses used to sign in to the service, account identifiers, timestamps showing when users created and last accessed their accounts, and various pieces of non-secret account metadata. The company insists the information that customers actually pay it to protect was beyond the intruder's reach. "At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker," 1Password said. Arguably more troubling is the revelation that the intruder gained access to 1Password's continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) infrastructure, which houses credentials used to keep its products running. The company says it has rotated or revoked potentially exposed credentials and that neither its apps nor its browser extensions were affected. 1Password hasn't explained how access to an employee's GitHub account enabled the attacker to deploy malicious code to its backend services, nor has it detailed the extent of the attacker's access to its software build and distribution infrastructure. The company did not respond to The Register's questions. The miscreant also got their hands on tokens embedded in emails sent to some customers as part of account invitations, provisioning, and recovery processes. These tokens aren't enough to access an account on their own, according to 1Password, as users must also authenticate via single sign-on or enter a verification code sent to their registered email address. The company says it specifically notified the small number of users with affected provisioning or recovery processes underway. It found no internal evidence of account takeovers using the exposed provisioning tokens. Still, the breach has prompted the password management biz to beef up those verification codes, replacing the six-digit numeric variety with ten-character alphanumeric codes to make brute-forcing them considerably more difficult. 1Password has booted the intruder out of its GitHub environment, revoked the stolen token, and rolled back the affected backend services to clean versions of the code. It's since shored up security around its development infrastructure and employees' devices, and brought in outside security specialists to review its handiwork. The incident recalls the first stage of LastPass's 2022 breach, when an attacker compromised its development environment and stole source code. Information obtained in that intrusion helped enable a second attack that exposed customer vault backups, including encrypted passwords. The UK Information Commission's Office slapped LastPass with a £1.2 million ($1.6 million) fine last December over the incident, which compromised the personal information of up to 1.6 million UK users. Among the regulator's gripes was that LastPass had fallen short of the higher standard of security expected of a company entrusted with people's passwords. Customers aren't being asked to change their account passwords or Secret Keys, neither of which 1Password stores, although the company is warning users to be on the lookout for phishing attempts. A list of email addresses belonging to people known to use a particular password manager is a handy thing for a phisher to have, especially when said password manager has just given them a plausible pretext for getting in touch. ®

item.title: UK Home Office waved through border system without a working fix for bad data
item.description: ICO reprimand follows failings that risked wrongful detention, with a temporary correction process taking more than a year to arrive
item.content:encoded: The Information Commission's Office (ICO) has reprimanded the UK Home Office over a border watchlist system launched without an effective way to correct inaccurate personal information. The regulator said the failings risked people being wrongly detained for additional checks at the UK border, potentially causing distress and other harm. The platform in question, Helios, was slated to replace its predecessor, Warnings Index, in September 2024 and despite an initial delay due to concerns over data quality, went live the following month. Both Helios and Warnings Index are watch-listing systems, designed to allow law enforcement officials – mainly but not exclusively Border Force – to check people's data against official records at the UK border. Helios's federated operating model, whereby the data sources are not centrally managed, yielded quicker results than Warnings Index, but contained a critical flaw in that operational staff could not alter incorrect records. Platform operators, such as Border Force officers, could not amend the data that feeds into it, neither after the fact nor in real time. This was not the case with Warnings Index, which had a dedicated team responsible for correcting data entries in real time. Under Helios, staff were supposed to report inaccuracies to the organization responsible for the relevant source data, which would make the correction. One slight problem: there was no established reporting system at the time Helios was launched on October 2. The platform went live anyway, as officials deemed the data integrity and security risks presented by Warnings Index to be greater than those of Helios. Just nine days passed before the Home Office's data protection officer had to submit a breach report after Helios operational staff said they didn't know how to request data corrections. During the time, Helios operators sent 87 data rectification requests to the Warnings Index correction team, despite it having no capability to make the required changes to the data. The Home Office later said that many other requests likely weren't logged as the proper processes were not in place, and that staff should have logged the issue through a ServiceNow IT ticket, as any other departmental civil servant with any kind of IT issue would have. But the Home Office also said that including personal data in those helpdesk tickets would itself constitute a data breach. The ICO said in its reprimand document [PDF] that it is "unclear" how such a reporting arrangement could realistically work in practice, given that a report would require details from a subject's record that required rectification as well as the new, accurate information that should be used to replace it. The Home Office's proposed workaround was to get operational staff to verbally read out said personal data over a phone call with the IT helpdesk – a procedure it described as possible "but cumbersome." It took the Home Office more than a year to implement a temporary data-rectification method, which involved a BX Data Query tile on the IT Now platform, allowing Helios operators to securely report data accuracy issues. The new method went live on October 25, 2025. By March 18, 2026, the Home Office said the new process had received more than 6,500 correction requests and around 5,000 records had been removed. The ICO said it "remains concerned" about the efficacy of this method, given that operators cannot include personal data in the tile report, but the regulator is satisfied the problem is at least in part fixed. The Home Office also said it was aware of an increase in customer complaints following Helios's launch, and around 800 cases in which people were delayed at the UK border pending additional checks. It was unable to attribute a specific number of these to Helios's technical issues, however. "The Home Office further stated that it was not aware of any data subjects suffering distress as a result of using its services at the UK border," the ICO's report stated. A Home Office spokesperson told us: "We take data protection extremely seriously. That is why we have co-operated fully with the Information Commissioner's Office. "We immediately removed all outdated records to minimize delays to passenger journeys and strengthened mechanisms to speed up updates. "Our processes will continue to be kept under review, ensuring we meet data protection obligations while protecting border security." Joanne Stones, investigations manager at the ICO, said: "People must be able to trust that decisions about their immigration status at the UK border are made with accurate, up to date information." She added: "They also have the right to expect that when information is inaccurate, there is a swift and efficient way for it to be corrected. "We recognize that federated systems like Helios present unique challenges and welcome the steps the Home Office has taken since this issue was identified. However, the Home Office must ensure that its permanent solution provides a robust and effective way to identify and correct inaccurate information without delay." The ICO's public sector enforcement policy favors guidance, reprimands, and other interventions, reserving fines for the most egregious cases. Its rationale is to avoid diverting money from public services and effectively punishing those affected twice. Fines have included £350,000 for a 2021 MoD email that exposed details of Afghan evacuation applicants, and £750,000 for the PSNI's 2023 disclosure of workforce information, including surnames, initials, ranks, and roles. The PSNI penalty was reduced from £5.6 million under the public sector approach. ®

item.title: The security of US water systems is even leakier than we thought
item.description: And intruders don't always need to exploit bugs to break in
item.content:encoded: American water systems are even less secure than we thought, according to a study of 236 technology vendors that provide gear to US drinking water, wastewater, and industrial water systems. The federal government has issued 4,014 security advisories for industrial control systems and cataloged 1,792 vulnerabilities known to have been exploited in cyberattacks. A new index, called Water Supply Chain Watch and published by exposure management firm Securin, however, found almost twice as many vulnerabilities as public records identified – including 20 exploited flaws that weren't even in the federal government's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. The security provider compared data on water-tech vendors with records from the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the FBI, and WaterISAC, drawing on CISA advisory data through November 20 and KEV catalog entries through November 23. It found that federal water advisories hit their highest level this year since 2020. However, the volume of security alerts isn't a reliable predictor of real-world attacks, the researchers noted. Five vendors – Rockwell Automation (58), Advantech (48), Schneider Electric (35), Siemens (26), and ABB (24) – account for 191 of the 376 water-tagged security advisories. The No. 2 firm, Advantech, accounted for the highest number of vulnerabilities rated critical, but none of the CVEs in its advisories appear in CISA's KEV catalog. Unitronics, on the other hand, accounted for only two water-tagged security advisories, but at least 75 of its controllers were compromised between November 2023 and January 2024 by attackers taking advantage of default or missing passwords. The report also highlights another disconnect between water-related CVEs and real-world cyberattacks, which don't always require attackers to exploit software bugs. The July intrusions, which security researchers suspect were the work of Iran-linked attackers, targeted more than 100 water systems, with incidents reported across at least 12 states, and involved poorly secured internet-connected controllers. According to Securin, 791 Rockwell MicroLogix 1400 controllers across multiple industries in the US were exposed to the internet as of November 17. Additionally, research by Forescout cited by the security shop found that most exposed Rockwell controllers in the US – seven in 10 – sit on mobile carrier networks, where poorly secured cellular modems can provide an entry point for attackers. A CISA advisory from July describes this technique: The authoring agencies observed Iranian-affiliated APT actors using several foreign-based IP addresses to access internet-facing PLCs manufactured by Rockwell Automation/Allen-Bradley, Schneider Electric, Siemens, and potentially other manufactured PLCs [T0883]. The actors used leased, third-party hosted infrastructure and manufacturers’ PLC programming software to connect to misconfigured victim PLCs. Inbound malicious traffic has been observed targeting PLC devices on the following ports: 44818, 2222, 102, and 502, as well as targeting modems on port 22. These cellular modems, often installed by third-party contractors, frequently aren’t documented. Unsurprisingly, the top recommendation for water utilities is to find every cellular modem in the environment, including those installed by contractors, make sure they aren’t exposed to the open internet, and put a gateway with multifactor authentication (MFA) in front of them to stop would-be intruders from gaining access via the modem and controller combo. “Water utilities are spending time and money fixing the vulnerabilities they're told to worry about,” Securin CEO Srinivas Mukkamala said in a statement. “Meanwhile, attackers are getting in through equipment nobody knew was connected or passwords nobody bothered to change.” ®

item.title: Microsoft's NTLM security changes trip up third-party logins
item.description: It's not our fault if you've implemented it wrong
item.content:encoded: Microsoft's November security updates can break authentication in some third-party applications and devices following changes to NTLM message signing. Affected systems include authentication proxy servers, single sign-on (SSO) products, and application packaging tools, the company's support notice says. The failures stem from products that claim to supply required information during NTLM authentication but return incomplete or empty data, Microsoft said: "An affected device might set the NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_TARGET_INFO flag in its CHALLENGE_MESSAGE but provide an empty or incomplete TargetInfo field." Administrators can use the notice's network trace and event log examples to identify affected products. For confirmed cases, the temporary workaround is to set the ClientAllowUnsignedNtlm Registry value to 1 on affected clients. This stops the client offering signing, backing out the new default rather than fixing the incompatible product. The recommended long-term options are a vendor update or Kerberos authentication, where supported. The value sits under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\MSV1_0 and defaults to 0, enabling clients to offer signing on non-anonymous connections. The NTLM changes arrived in the November 10 update as phase 1 in a 2-phase process. In phase 1, "Windows client devices begin offering NTLM signing on all connections by default. Servers accept both signed and unsigned clients. Auditing events identify clients not using signing." Phase 2, scheduled for May 2027, will make Windows servers require NTLM signing by default. "Clients that do not offer signing will be rejected by secure servers," Microsoft stated. Ominously, Microsoft warned that it "might remove the registry keys at a future date," so the company is not kidding about the temporary workaround thing. The additional protections were added to address CVE-2026-118737, a vulnerability in which "improper verification of cryptographic signature in Windows Remote Procedure Call Runtime allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network." NTLM is on Microsoft's hit list, having joined the Deprecated Features list in 2024. It dates back to the era of Windows NT, and Microsoft has made clear that it wants customers to move to Kerberos, which became the default in 2000. Even so, NTLM lingers on. Deprecation doesn't remove Microsoft's obligation to secure NTLM while it remains in supported Windows releases. For administrators, though, the immediate task is identifying incompatible products before temporary exceptions give way to stricter enforcement. ®

item.title: US Treasury financial crimes unit becomes latest fed breach victim
item.description: FinCEN takes systems offline and extends filing deadlines while investigating 'unauthorized access'
item.content:encoded: The US Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has taken some systems offline following unauthorized access, disrupting regulatory filings for financial institutions. An alert has gone up on FinCEN's Bank Secrecy Act E-Filing website, as shown in this archived copy, informing those who need to submit reports that they might not be able to while the agency deals with the situation. FinCEN not only enforces compliance with the Bank Secrecy Act and associated regulations but also collects and analyzes financial intelligence for sharing with other US agencies and foreign government partners. In other words, it has some juicy info in its databases. “FinCEN is investigating a cybersecurity incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems,” the alert states. “As a proactive measure, FinCEN has taken some systems offline.” FinCEN hasn't said which systems intruders accessed, but clues in the deadline extension notice the agency posted alongside the warning suggest the disruption affects its reporting services for banks and other financial institutions required to submit reports detailing certain financial transactions and suspicious activity that may indicate money laundering or other illicit activity. FinCEN's Secure Data Transfer Mode, one method of submitting those reports, appears to be affected, as do services companies use to submit beneficial ownership information reports and individuals use to update their FinCEN identifiers. Eligible organizations and individuals with filings or updates due from November 18 through December 29 now have until December 30 to submit them. The Register has learned that there’s no evidence of any unauthorized access to Bank Secrecy Act data or beneficial ownership databases. That said, the investigation is ongoing - so that could change. “Treasury is working with the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and third-party forensic examiners to determine the scope and impact of the incident,” a FinCEN official told us in an email. Several US government agencies have experienced cybersecurity incidents in recent months, including the ATF and the FBI, and reports emerged this week that intruders had also compromised an unclassified CIA system. While US authorities have linked previous cyberespionage campaigns to Chinese or other government-backed groups, financially motivated criminal groups have also targeted federal agencies. As the FinCEN breach is still under investigation, the agency hasn’t stated who may be involved and for what purpose. ®

item.title: Gatwick drop-off customers' personal data exposed in supplier breach
item.description: AutoPay login and vehicle records affected, alongside limited payment information and customer service emails
item.content:encoded: London Gatwick Airport has warned customers that a breach of its drop-off payment service exposed personal information and, in limited cases, payment records. A notification email seen by The Register identifies the affected system as AutoPay, operated by ParkPark and used by Gatwick's drop-off zone manager, Times24 UK Limited. AutoPay lets drivers register their vehicle and payment details in advance so drop-off charges are collected automatically. Gatwick told us it was unable to provide details about how many customers were affected by the breach, or how far back the affected records go. The email said most affected customers would have only some of the listed data exposed. The could include names, home addresses, cities, postcodes, contact details, and AutoPay login credentials such as email addresses and bcrypt-hashed passwords were affected. Other records implicated in the breach include details of vehicles linked to AutoPay accounts, those vehicles' entry and exit times at Times24-managed parking locations, and vehicle registrations. The email also states that payment records, including amounts, card types, card expiry dates, payment references, transaction statuses, transaction IDs, and drop-off locations and times were affected, but a Gatwick spokesperson said this applied only to "very limited cases." Again, in a minority of cases, "some limited emails between the customer service team and customers" were also exposed, the email stated. Gatwick said Times24 "immediately suspended" AutoPay after detecting the intrusion. The service remains disabled while the investigation continues. Airport officials are overseeing the response with outside cybersecurity specialists. Gatwick warned of possible disruption to its website but said flights were unaffected. Customers can still use Gatwick's drop-off zones, although they'll have to use alternative payment methods, and all other airport services are still operating as usual. The notification email urged customers to exercise caution when receiving communications from Gatwick, Times24, AutoPay, or ParkPark, especially those that ask for payment or bank details. Times24, which operates across more than 200 car parks in the UK, did not immediately respond to our request for more information. Dray Agha, senior manager at Huntress's tactical response division, warned that criminals could use the data for convincing scams long after news coverage of the breach has faded. "The real damage often comes after the breach," he said. "Criminals rarely use stolen data straight away; they'll wait until the headlines fade, then send a text about a 'parking fine' or an email offering a 'refund' that references a real booking. Even partial card details add a layer of credibility that makes people far more likely to hand over the rest. "Gatwick customers should assume any unexpected message about their parking could be a scam, check directly with the airport, and keep a close eye on their bank statements over the coming months." ®

item.title: This could mess with Thanksgiving, says VMware as it drops third critical patch bundle in a week
item.description: Four more critical vulns, including another unauthorized access flaw in vCenter
item.content:encoded: VMware has issued its third critical security advisory in a week, this time to warn of four critical flaws and address a total of 23 issues. VMSA-2026-0011 landed on November 24, just five days after two other advisories. VMware’s FAQ for the new advisory includes the following remarks: Because of coordinated disclosure and release pipeline timing this VMSA comes on the heels of VMSA-2026-0009, and atop a major holiday in the United States. The security vulnerability landscape is more dynamic than ever; please know that while we acknowledge this timing is not optimal, your ability to operate and maintain a secure environment amidst modern, AI-assisted threats is paramount to us. Make of that what you will as you ponder how and when to patch the four critical flaws, including the 9.8-rated CVE-2026-123903, which allows a malicious actor to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to vCenter, the management tool VMware users rely on to manage hosts and VMs. This is the third 9.8-rated authentication issue VMware has fixed in vCenter since July. Two of the other critical flaws in this new advisory allow an attacker to run code on an ESX host, earning the bugs a 9.8 rating. CVE-2026-123910 makes that possible thanks to a heap out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the I/O filter service, while CVE-2026-123911 is a use-after-free vulnerability. The other critical flaw, CVE-2026-123912, can result in a guest escape from VMware’s desktop Workstation and Fusion desktop hypervisors. It’s also present in VMware’s ESX hypervisor, but attackers thankfully can’t escape that product’s sandbox. This one’s easy to mitigate because the problem is in a USB controller that users can turn off. Most of the other flaws require installation of updated software. There’s a little good news in that some of the software updates VMware issued last week include fixes for the newly disclosed flaws. But there are still plenty of fresh fixes to apply, across ten products: ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, VMware tools, Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, the Telco Cloud Platform, Telco Cloud Infrastructure, and the VMware Avi Load Balancer. VMware’s advisory thanks external researchers for finding and reporting most of the flaws. The Broadcom business unit is known to be a member of Project Glasswing, the Anthropic-run effort to use the Mythos model to find flaws that has seen many vendors dramatically increase the number of patches they produce. In past years, VMware has often published considerably more than this year’s 11 security advisories. With five weeks left in the year, perhaps vAdmins need to worry Christmas might also get complicated. ®

item.title: 'We are not ShinyHunters,' says criminal hacking crew that looks and acts just like ShinyHunters
item.description: Nothing to see here…
item.content:encoded: Inception, a new data theft and extortion gang that security researchers have theorized is a rebrand of the ShinyHunters group, “reject[s] this attribution” and claims it has no affiliation with any prior cybercrime enterprise. In a lengthy statement posted Tuesday and shared on X, the extortionists insist that they are a new group, with new operators, and that their alleged social engineering attacks aren’t copying anyone - but rather just abusing the weakest link in an organization’s security: “a human being holding a phone.” The rant follows a Monday report by Okta Threat Intelligence - along with social media speculation since Inception’s inception last week - that the newly emerged group is very likely ShinyHunters with a different name. Okta’s researchers based their analysis on the two groups’ shared infrastructure, plus Inception’s nearly identical tactics: voice phishing, during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA) requests. Inception apparently took offense to this. “We would like to address this once, clearly, and only once,” the crims' statement says. “We are not ShinyHunters. We were never ShinyHunters. We are Inception.” The gang argues that its overlapping domain registrars, hosting providers, and DNS services don’t prove anything. These are commodity services, “available to anyone who can pay for them,” Inception wrote. Plus, their similar methodologies don't necessarily make Inception a reboot. “That is not theft of tradecraft,” they wrote. “It is acknowledgment of a good idea – the same way every group after LockBit used a leak site, and nobody called them LockBit.” “Inception is a new group, with new operators, our own objectives, and our own name,” the statement continues. “What we share with the past is plumbing.” To be fair, the new crime crew has every reason to distance itself from ShinyHunters. That gang’s September FBI hack - plus several earlier digital heists during which the criminals stole information belonging to millions of people, including cancer patients, university and K-12 students - put a massive target on its collective backs. And while at least three ShinyHunters suspects were arrested in September and October, there's no confirmation that authorities have dismantled the entire operation. Plus, as a ShinyHunters spokesperson told The Register in an earlier interview, they and others in the crew started off as GnosticPlayers before rebranding as ShinyHunters in 2020 - so a reboot isn’t beyond the realm of possibility. Inception, for its part, says it “will not comment further on the ghost of ShinyHunters,” and it has its own work to do. And by work, it means copying ShinyHunters' playbook, stealing corporate data, and extorting victim companies for massive sums of money.®

item.title: An AI coding agent, a browser, and a Mac tool found a financial firm's access key in under 6 minutes
item.description: No sophisticated malware or attack framework required
item.content:encoded: A Romanian hacker, armed with only an open source coding agent, a Chrome browser, and a Mac, tried multiple ways to break into a financial services firm, ultimately found an access key - luckily, it was a decoy - and carried out an entire (almost) attack in under six minutes. It’s a stark reminder that miscreants don’t need sophisticated malware - as in the Binance heist - or AI pen-testing tools like ARTEX to carry out intrusions into critical networks. Open source coding agents, and specifically OpenCode in this case, also work just fine. “What surprised me most was how little it took and the toolkit: a free coding agent, the curl that comes with every Mac and an ordinary Chrome, all from one laptop,” Jesta co-founder and CTO Lior Finkelshtein told The Register. “Until now I thought that we had more time until tools like OpenCode are used in offensive operations. This incident shows us that it's already in use in the field, and we will probably see more of that in the future.” Jesta is a Tel Aviv-based security startup that builds defensive tools to detect and stop autonomous AI attacks. In a report shared exclusively with The Register, Finkelshtein documented an attempted intrusion targeting a major financial services company that’s also a Jesta customer - the security shop declined to say which one. Jesta’s investigation into the incident determined that someone in Bucharest downloaded a free AI coding agent called OpenCode and pointed it at the financial services customer on November 16 at 4:24:57 a.m. ET. 'Nothing in OpenCode was built for hacking' OpenCode is an open source coding agent that lets users connect to more than 200 model providers or local models, including Anthropic’s Claude models, OpenAI’s GPTs, Google’s Gemini, DeepSeek, and Z.ai’s GLM. Jesta doesn’t know which model the attacker used, as there was nothing in the traffic that named the model. OpenCode's web fetch tool, however, did name itself, so Jesta knows the attacker used this coding agent - not a scanner - to do the dirty work. “Nothing in OpenCode was built for hacking,” Finkelshtein said in a Tuesday report about the agent-led attack. But, he added, nothing in the coding agent “stops you from pointing it at someone else's website either. When you do, the agent goes through the site the same way it goes through code. It reads, tries something, reads the result and tries the next thing, for as long as you let it run.” That’s what it did in this operation, which took less than six minutes and cost the human operator nothing. The first call came from a Chrome browser on a Mac, requesting the front page of one of the financial firm’s systems. The site refused it, and six seconds later, the same IPv6 address in Bucharest, on an ordinary DIGI Romania business line, tried again. It used the same Chrome version, but said it was an Android Pixel 10 phone (it wasn’t) to see if the site would let a phone in (it didn’t). After failing to gain access through the front page, the agent asked the system for its API definition, which was also refused. Five seconds later, it tried a different address - this one was a decoy set up by Jesta - and it answered the agent, providing the readable file defining how the API works. The agent read the document, and 13 seconds later followed a link it contained. At 4:26:01 a.m. ET, Jesta’s defenses marked the website visitor as an AI agent, opened a case, and from here on out, everything the agent accessed was contained inside a fake environment designed to trick intruders. This included a phony key, which the attacker then used to attempt to break into the company’s systems. “It worked like a developer,” Finkelshtein said about the coding agent. “It read the API docs and did what they said. It found a key and used it. It checked whether the lock was real, then made up a key of its own and tried that. None of the threat feeds the customer has knew the address, so a blocklist would never have stopped it. The bar for doing this is now installing an app. Think about how many people can do that.” 'No blocklist would have helped' In addition to OpenCode, the attacker used only Chrome 157, both in desktop and mobile modes, and curl/8.7.1, a command-line tool that has shipped with every Mac since macOS 15. The agent passed information between the three tools. It included the planted key in a command-line request and then tested three scenarios – using the decoy key, no key, and a fabricated key – to determine whether what it found in the API documentation was legit. It also tried multiple URLs using the browser. While it ultimately identified a valid endpoint, it attempted to read from one that accepts only data submissions, so its request was blocked again. Five minutes and 44 seconds after the first request, it gave up, and the logs haven’t detected any activity from this same intruder since then. The security shop and its customer disclosed the activity to law enforcement and told us it’s “being handled.” While the attacker wasn’t able to steal anything in this attempt, security teams still need to take note, according to Finkelshtein. “No blocklist would have helped” detect the malicious traffic, he explained. “Most security tools still decide by asking whether an address is known to be bad, and for this one the answer was no. If that key had been real, it would have been in.” Instead of blocklists, Finkelshtein suggests paying attention to what the visitor does. In this case, several of its actions gave it away - including following a link that only existed inside an API doc, using a desktop browser and a fake phone, then curl, all from the same address within minutes, and trying multiple keys - including one with a made up name and then no key - within seconds. “Open source lets anyone build software without a big team,” Finkelshtein wrote in the Tuesday blog. “AI is doing the same for hacking. The skill is in the model, the model is a setting, and the person giving the instructions doesn't need to know how any of it works.” ®

item.title: CrowdStrike splashes $44B on Zscaler, customers brace for the bill
item.description: Record-breaking cybersecurity deal promises tighter integration, but sysadmins fear higher prices and vendor lock-in
item.content:encoded: CrowdStrike has agreed to buy Zscaler for $43.9 billion in what would be the biggest cybersecurity acquisition on record, and customers are already bracing for pricier renewals. The all-stock deal, announced on Monday, will see Zscaler shareholders receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for every share they own, representing a 34 percent premium on Friday's closing price. The transaction dwarfs even Google's $32 billion acquisition of cloud security upstart Wiz. Buying Zscaler gives CrowdStrike a sizeable foothold in the network security market, where it will be going up against the likes of Palo Alto Networks and Fortinet. The plan is to combine Falcon's endpoint protection capabilities with Zscaler's zero-trust network security technology, giving customers a single platform for securing devices and the connections between them. Naturally, there's an AI angle to the biggest cyber deal in history. CrowdStrike reckons owning both technologies will allow it to keep tabs on what AI agents are doing on corporate devices, where they're connecting, and what data they're getting their hands on. CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz described the proposed combination as "cybersecurity’s operating system." The acquisition also gives CrowdStrike's salespeople plenty to get excited about. Around 8,000 Zscaler customers don't currently buy CrowdStrike's wares, and the companies already have more than 2,000 customers in common. CrowdStrike reckons it can boost its annualized revenue by around $1 billion within 30 months of closing the deal by selling more products to the two companies' existing customers. Some of those customers, however, don't sound particularly keen on being cross-sold to. Over on Reddit's r/sysadmin subreddit, news of the purchase was met with a familiar set of concerns from IT professionals who've lived through big-ticket enterprise software acquisitions before. "As a zscaler customer, this does worry me. Cost increase, forced move to Falcon, integration issues, etc," wrote one sysadmin. Another, whose organization already uses both vendors' products, added: "I think they're both great products but I imagine they'll jack up the price for our next renewal. Fun." CrowdStrike intends to make Zscaler's products available through its Falcon Flex licensing scheme, which allows customers to commit to a certain level of spending and pick and choose the products they deploy. Monday's acquisition announcement didn't spell out what the deal would mean for customers who want to continue using Zscaler alongside a rival endpoint security product. Others raised concerns about the fate of Red Canary, the managed detection and response specialist snapped up by Zscaler in August 2025. CrowdStrike already operates a competing service in Falcon Complete. There may also be some nervous employees at both companies. CrowdStrike is targeting $500 million in annual cost savings within two years of completing the acquisition, identifying datacenter infrastructure, supplier spending, and wider operations as areas where it can trim the fat. Neither company disclosed whether that would involve job cuts. Then there's the matter of putting more of the world's corporate security infrastructure in the hands of CrowdStrike, whose botched July 2024 software update took down an estimated 8.5 million Windows machines, grounding flights and disrupting hospitals, banks, and businesses worldwide. The incident gave IT departments a rather painful lesson in the risks of relying heavily on a single technology supplier. The deal is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal 2028, assuming regulators and Zscaler shareholders give it the green light. Zscaler founder and CEO Jay Chaudhry will remain in charge of the business and take a seat on CrowdStrike's board. CrowdStrike reckons the combined business will have more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue when the deal closes. Judging by the reaction from some customers, they'll be keeping a particularly close eye on how much of that revenue comes from them. ®

item.title: European Commission confirms personal data stolen in AI-assisted cyberattack
item.description: EU Academy names and email addresses exposed, with users warned via website notice rather than contacted directly
item.content:encoded: The European Commission has confirmed that hackers made off with personal data in the AI-assisted cyberattack disclosed last week, but has relied on a website notice rather than contacting affected users directly. Speaking at a press briefing on Monday, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed that EU Academy, an online learning platform offering courses on EU policies and initiatives, was among the systems compromised during the cyber campaign targeting the bloc's executive arm. The stolen data includes the names and email addresses of people outside the EU institutions, though the Commission has yet to figure out how many users are affected or whether other personal information was compromised. Public access to the platform has been disabled as a precaution. Despite confirming the theft, the Commission hasn't contacted affected individuals directly. Instead, it has posted a notice on the EU Academy website, a decision Regnier defended when quizzed by reporters on Monday. "There was no reach out to individual users, but rather a general message to all users on the website out of transparency," Regnier said. The notice warns users that they could find themselves on the receiving end of spearphishing attacks, impersonation attempts, and spam as a result of the breach. The Commission is also advising users not to hand over personal information to anyone who contacts them claiming to be involved in EU Academy activities. The trouble with notifying users via the EU Academy website is that they've already been told not to come back until January. A separate notice says the platform will be offline from November 11 through January 14, 2027, while the Commission rebuilds it. When it reopens, users will have to register again, and any record of their previous coursework won't be transferred. The Register has asked the Commission whether the downtime and the requirement to create new accounts are connected to the cyberattack.A spokesperson didn't answer those points. The Commission has informed the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS), the watchdog responsible for policing EU institutions' handling of personal data. The EDPS told The Register that the Commission had notified it of the incident in stages, but declined to say whether it considered the Commission's approach to notifying affected users sufficient. "I can confirm that the EDPS has been informed and notified in phases by the European Commission," a spokesperson said. "Our colleagues remain in regular contact with EC services on the cyberattack and its implication. This is an ongoing case, so I cannot tell you more at this stage on the actions the EDPS might take as supervisory authority." The Commission first publicly acknowledged the cyberattack last Thursday, almost a month after suspicious activity was detected on October 22. Several internal applications were temporarily taken offline, and while most had since been restored, some remained unavailable at the time of Thursday's briefing. The Commission has confirmed the attackers used an AI-assisted hacking tool, and the incident comes amid mounting concerns over ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration testing framework that security researchers have linked to large-scale cyber espionage campaigns. More than a month after the Commission first spotted the intrusion, Regnier was unwilling to say on Monday whether its security teams had finally seen off the hackers. "As long as the investigation is ongoing, I will not make any conclusive statements at this stage on where we are," he said. ®

item.title: Orgs that leak data 'prioritize corporate interests over customers' says Have I Been Pwned’s Troy Hunt
item.description: Leakers move through denial, bargaining, delay, legal threats, then claiming Hunt is the real villain
item.content:encoded: Troy Hunt, the founder of data breach reporting site Have I Been Pwned (HIBP), has revealed how organizations respond when he informs them they’ve leaked data – if they respond at all. Hunt gave Anthropic’s Claude access to an email inbox containing over eight years of his email correspondence and then asked the AI to write a post summarising them, a method he said “was the best way to highlight the behaviors I keep seeing across many breaches and subsequent disclosure efforts.” Writing in person, Hunt described those behaviors as “standoffish behavior, deliberate delays, heavy involvement from lawyers, and a constant theme: prioritizing corporate interests over those of their customers.” Once Claude takes over writing duties, it opens with the observation that Hunt sent his standard notification email to 73 organizations between March 2018 and November 2026 and also used website contact forms. Claude/Hunt focuses on the breach notifications that don’t go well, for example when first contact “often goes nowhere” because “many organisations have no obvious way to report a security incident.” Some organizations Hunt contacted logged his notifications as customer support requests. “In one case, Troy received three automated surveys asking him to rate the support he'd received,” Claude wrote, before observing “A message that an organization’s customer data is being traded among criminals ended up in the same queue as a question about a late delivery.” Once someone at victim organization gets the message, a common response is to say they can find no evidence of the breach. Others try to play down the incident, saying it was only a website defacement or that Hunt is re-reporting a previous breach the victim has already disclosed. If an organization accepts Hunt is probably onto something, it typically says it needs to investigate the matter. Claude’s take on Hunt’s mails suggests he responds by pointing out that this is an irresponsible approach, because while the investigation takes place, “people whose data has been taken don't know they need to change a password or watch for phishing.” Next, victims send in the lawyers who ask if their employer or client is legally required to reveal the breach. Hunt typically replies by saying it is up to the victim to decide if the incident meets the threshold that triggers mandatory disclosure requirements under local laws, but that he intends to notify HIBP users regardless. Victims don’t like hearing that and respond in three ways: Calling to discuss disclosure, rather than committing to it; Asking to see the wording HIBP will use in its disclosure, a request that sees Hunt refer the victim to the HIBP site for examples of the thousand-plus breach reports already on the site; Arguing that disclosure, not the breach, is the real harm. Hunt/Claude suggests that each argument victims use to avoid disclosure “sounds reasonable on its own,” but argues “Together, they mean the people most affected by the breach are the last to hear about it.” The post also reports on some better interactions, such as a small booking platform that was initially skeptical about Hunt’s report, then admitted he was right and acted swiftly to inform customers. A European travel app hardened its systems, rotated its keys, and published a disclosure. “Troy held off loading the data so he could link to their statement, and thanked them for their transparency,” according to the Claude-generated text. The bot’s analysis also offers examples of when breach notifications go well. “Someone with authority over security answered quickly,” Claude concluded. “They treated Troy's data as help rather than as a threat. They told their customers what they knew, even when they didn't know everything yet, and updated the details later. None of them needed lawyers to manage the conversation.” Hunt appears to have asked Claude to offer its opinion of his email trove. “I don't think the main obstacle to disclosure is technical, or even legal,” the post states. “It's about incentives. For the organization, every day without a public statement is a day without bad headlines.” Hunt also said he won’t make a habit of having AI write his content, but said Claude “absolutely nails it!” Unlike many of the orgs Hunt contacted. ®

item.title: Cisco and OpenAI pitch eBPF kernel plugins as the way to tame the patchpocalypse
item.description: ‘Shirudo’ project promises to whip up compensating controls in a hurry
item.content:encoded: Cisco and OpenAI have released an open-source tool called Shirudo to implement compensating controls in Linux, potentially improving security for users who can’t quickly patch newly discovered software flaws. Shirudo relies on eBPF, the technology that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs in the Linux kernel. eBPF programs are effectively kernel plug-ins but don’t get unrestricted access to system resources. Developers have mostly used eBPF to create network functions that enable things like the open source Kubernetes observability and security tool Cilium, a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project. Cisco and OpenAI think eBPF can help organizations cope with the flood of 100,000-plus software flaws reported this year, many after the debut of AI-powered bug finders. The increased volume of flaws, and patches to fix them, is a problem for many organizations which already struggle to test fixes or find change windows in which to implement them. That problem has seen greater interest in “compensating controls” – changes to applications or infrastructure that harden them against flaws or malware, without requiring a patch. With Shirudo, Cisco and OpenAI are suggesting two things: The privileges eBPF programs enjoy make them a fine way to implement compensating controls for Linux; Agents should scan your infrastructure for vulnerabilities, then use tools like OpenAI’s Codex to write compensating controls as eBPF programs at machine speed. “Shirudo” is apparently the Japanese word for “shield,” so Cisco and OpenAI have called the eBPF programs the tool creates “shields.” The two companies envision humans checking every shield Shirudo creates before putting it into production. Shirudo is open source and available here. The two companies say they’ve already demonstrated it could mitigate the recently discovered flaws in Java without requiring downtime for an Elasticsearch implementation. Cisco and OpenAI are not alone in advocating for compensating controls. Third-party software maintenance outfits like Rimini Street have used them for years to protect software when their clients no longer have the right to access patches. VMware has introduced “virtual patching.” Palo Alto Networks and Rapid 7 also like this approach, and offer automation to develop controls. Where Cisco and OpenAI differ is their decision to make Shirudo open source, and their ambition that other players adapt and advance it. That offer is not entirely altruistic, as if Shirudo takes off it could create more demand for Codex. Cisco’s angle comes from the fact it owns Isovalent, an early champion of eBPF and the creator of both Cilium and the Tetragon sub-project on which Shirudo is based. Switchzilla is using eBPF in other products, so normalizing its use through an open source project can’t hurt. ®

item.title: Inception - possibly a ShinyHunters reboot - claims seven victims in a week
item.description: Whatever they call themselves these days: be on the lookout for voice phishing attempts
item.content:encoded: Don't mind the recent arrests. The ShinyHunters extortion gang may still be operating, just under the new name of Inception, according to Okta's threat intelligence group. ShinyHunters is the brash cybercriminal group that, most recently, breached rival gang Clop before hacking the FBI, resulting in at least three arrests of key suspects in September and October. The crims - and their old data leak site - have since gone dark. “While this threat cluster has changed their brand affiliation, the operators remain active in targeting organizations with voice phishing attacks and account takeovers resulting in data theft and extortion,” Okta threat hunters Moussa Diallo and Katie Nickels said on Monday. Okta tracks this threat cluster as O-UNC-053 - the “O-UNC” prefix stands for an Okta Uncategorized cluster, and it uses this label before formally attributing the activity to a named threat group. While Okta hasn't formally confirmed O-UNC-053 to be the same crime crew as ShinyHunters, the identity and access management provider’s researchers note that it does use nearly identical social engineering tactics: voice phishing, during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA). Plus, they note: O-UNC-053 operators change the themes of their phishing domains about every four to six weeks, and they also post claimed victims on ShinyHunters’ data leak site. In November, however, organizations targeted by O-UNC-053 began appearing on a new data leak site branded as Inception and not ShinyHunters. The first five - Advanced Micro Devices, Cigna Healthcare, Paychex, PepsiCo, and Henry Schein - appeared November 17 on the site, and all were marked “leaked.” Soon after, security maven Dominic Alvieri questioned if Inception was linked to ShinyHunters. “ShinyHunters are not all in jail,” he wrote on social media. On November 19, AutoZone appeared on the site, with Inception again claiming to have leaked the auto-parts retailer's files. On Saturday, EV technology firm Lucid Group joined the claimed victims. None of the seven companies have confirmed breaches, and none responded to The Register’s inquiries. We will update this story when we receive more information. Okta Threat Intelligence “is unable to validate if published data is authentic,” the researchers said in response to our questions. In the Monday report, the Okta team does note that Inception’s new data leak site listings “included multiple targets for which Okta Threat Intelligence previously observed O-UNC-053 infrastructure registration.” The infrastructure was registered between six and 19 days before Inception listed the companies on its leak site, and this gap “is consistent with prior shifts from Com-affiliated actors,” Diallo and Nickels added. The Com (short for community) is a loosely knit network of online groups whose young members participate in a range of illicit activities including hacking, swatting, digital extortion, real-life shootings, and other physical violence. Many security researchers consider ShinyHunters to be connected to The Com, along with groups such as Scattered Spider and LAPSUS$, with overlapping memberships and shared infrastructure. “Before and after the change in DLS publication, O-UNC-053 maintained consistent infrastructure and TTPs, leading us to assess that the cluster has very likely changed their brand affiliation,” the Okta researchers wrote. “We cannot currently make a high confidence assessment as to whether O-UNC-053 is operating the DLS themselves or is partnering with another extortion actor.” Regardless, members of the group formerly known as ShinyHunters and/or O-UNC-053 are still roaming the internet, looking for new victims, and conducting voice phishing attacks to steal data and then extort victims' companies for exorbitant sums of money. Consider yourself warned - and turn on phishing-resistant MFA.®

item.title: Bluetooth brakes are broken as researchers find anyone can control them
item.description: Security fixes are available for two Elecbrakes models, but an older controller remains vulnerable and unpatched
item.content:encoded: Imagine something as mission-critical as the brakes on a trailer being vulnerable to unauthorized control. One Australian manufacturer made the interesting choice of building Bluetooth into a trailer brake controller without adequately securing its critical braking functions. Anyone within Bluetooth range of an unpatched Elecbrakes trailer controller could potentially trigger its brakes or apply more braking force than intended, without needing to authenticate. The discovery comes courtesy of a pair of security researchers from Element Digital, Patrick Forck and Jeremy McCarthy. Their investigation began earlier this year when Forck was driving down the road and noticed that his physical Elecbrakes In-Car Remote had connected to someone else's trailer without pairing or prompting him. “It had connected mid-drive, without pairing or a prompt, to a brake controller that wasn’t mine, on a trailer I’d never seen, belonging to a driver who had no idea,” the researchers wrote. That one-off connection triggered a full-scale investigation by the pair. For those unfamiliar with trailer brake controllers, these devices are commonly used on larger trailers. Australian manufacturer Elecbrakes sells such controllers in Australia and New Zealand. Depending on jurisdiction, trailers over a certain weight are required to have their own braking system, which Elecbrakes manufactures. Elecbrakes offers two versions that are designed to be easier to install than traditional controllers: One that’s mounted in a vehicle, and one that is mounted directly on a trailer. That trailer-mounted unit can receive Bluetooth commands from the Elecbrakes smartphone app or a separate in-car remote. Given the importance of such control units to road safety, it’s easy to imagine how serious such a vulnerability could be if it proved to be easy to exploit, and boy, did it. Forck and McCarthy admitted they’re infrastructure security guys, not software devs, so they turned to Claude Code to dissect a decompiled copy of the Elecbrakes app, which Claude was happy to oblige. “What came back from the analysis was a map of the device’s entire Bluetooth GATT profile: 47 characteristics across four services, commands sent as plain unencrypted byte arrays, no checksums, no sequence numbers,” the researchers noted. To make matters worse, there was no authentication required for critical braking commands, even though other Bluetooth functions required pairing. Claude then built a web app that ran in Chrome which was able to access the Bluetooth controls for a nearby Elecbrakes system, and they were able to modify practically every aspect of brake control on a unit owned by one of them. Pairing failed on a few attempts, but not where it mattered: It allowed the connection without issue for actual brake control. They sent a few bytes to the brake control characteristic, and were shocked. “The electromagnetic hum at the brake drums was immediate and, frankly, a little sickening,” the pair said. “It said yes to four bytes from a total stranger then energised several tonnes’ worth of brakes and reported back that it had done so, pleased with itself.” Further experiments managed to modify braking strength based on deceleration speed as well, making it so that the trailer acted unpredictably based on the amount of force a driver applied to stop their vehicle. To say this is worse than a typical internet-connected device bug is to put it mildly - it even earned a trio of CVEs from CISA, with two of them scoring a CVSS of 9.6. “The attack surface is ‘anyone within Bluetooth range,’ the skill required is ‘can write four bytes,’ and the victim selection is ‘optional,’ ” Forck and McCarthy said. The fact AI was able to get them to that point in just a couple of days is even more concerning, they added. “This kind of research used to require a fairly rare and specific skill set,” the pair noted. “It now requires curiosity, a device you own, and an AI that can read bytecode faster than any human.” Luckily, they appear to have been dealing with a relatively responsive company in Elecbrakes - patches have been deployed for both the in-car and trailer-mounted models of their brake controllers. Installation is a manual process, we note, so if you own a controller from the company, be sure to stop and install the update. Unfortunately, Elecbrakes has a third controller out there that hasn’t been manufactured in several years, and it got skipped in the patching process. Owners of an ELBC2000 should be aware that their controller is still vulnerable, and there’s no patch available yet, as the vendor didn’t confirm that the ELBC2000 was vulnerable until the end of October, after it faced pressure from the researchers. Following publication, the firm told us, "Elecbrakes takes the safety and security of its products seriously. Our engineering team reproduced and validated the cybersecurity vulnerability reported by the researchers. A safety risk assessment considered the likelihood of injury under specific scenarios. It concluded that, when a user is actively connected to their own controller through the Elecbrakes app or remote in line with product instructions, the cybersecurity vulnerability identified in the research is not present." ®

item.title: Critical Cisco remote code execution bug under attack
item.description: CISA, F6 sound the alarm after PoC exploit made public
item.content:encoded: Attackers are currently exploiting a critical vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-76466 in Cisco Expressway that allows them to remotely execute commands as root without any authentication, according to warnings from the US government and security researchers.
